days.title: Cell Membrane Structure
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the fluid mosaic model of the membrane.
  • Identify the components of the membrane.
  • Explain the functions of each component.
  • Relate structure to selective permeability.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Fluid mosaic model — describes membrane as a fluid bilayer with embedded proteins.
  • Phospholipid bilayer — two layers of phospholipids.
  • Amphipathic — having both hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions.

📚 Lesson Content

A. The Fluid Mosaic Model

Proposed by Singer and Nicolson (1972). The membrane is a dynamic structure — phospholipids and proteins move laterally.

B. Components

ComponentFunction
PhospholipidsForm the bilayer barrier
Integral proteinsTransport, channels, receptors
Peripheral proteinsSignaling, structural support
CholesterolRegulates fluidity
Glycolipids/GlycoproteinsCell recognition, adhesion

C. Selective Permeability

The membrane allows some substances to pass but blocks others. Small nonpolar molecules (O₂, CO₂) cross easily; ions and large polar molecules need transport proteins.

💬 Let's Discuss

This week we look at the plasma membrane again, this time as a gatekeeper. To understand how things cross it, you first need to understand why the membrane forms at all.

A phospholipid is amphipathic: its phosphate head is polar and attracted to water (hydrophilic), while its two fatty-acid tails are nonpolar and avoid water (hydrophobic). Put phospholipids in water and they arrange themselves automatically into a bilayer — heads facing the watery inside and outside of the cell, tails hidden in the middle. No energy is needed; it is the same reason oil and water separate. If the membrane is punctured slightly, it seals itself.

That oily middle is the key to transport. Small, nonpolar molecules such as O₂, CO₂ and steroid hormones dissolve in the tails and pass straight through. Ions (Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻) and large polar molecules such as glucose are blocked; they need help from membrane proteins. Integral proteins cross the whole bilayer and form channels and carriers. Peripheral proteins stay on one surface and work in signaling or as anchors. Glycoproteins and glycolipids carry sugar chains that serve as identity tags, and cholesterol keeps fluidity steady across temperatures.

So the structure explains the function: the bilayer makes the membrane selectively permeable, and the proteins decide which other substances get through and how.

Common mistake: calling the whole phospholipid "hydrophobic." Only the tails are. If you remember the head "loves" water and the tails "fear" it, you can predict how the bilayer forms.

pairs.why: Phospholipids arrange into two layers that form the basic membrane.
Integral proteins span the bilayer and act as channels or carriers.
Peripheral proteins sit on one face and help in signaling and support.
Cholesterol buffers membrane fluidity across temperatures.
Glycoproteins carry sugar chains used for recognition.
Amphipathic molecules have both a water-loving and a water-fearing part.

scenarios.explanation: The phospholipid bilayer is the basic barrier.

scenarios.text: Helps the membrane stay fluid at low temperatures.
scenarios.explanation: Cholesterol prevents phospholipids from packing too tightly in the cold.

scenarios.text: Acts as a channel for ions.
scenarios.explanation: Ions cross through integral channel proteins.

scenarios.explanation: Glycoproteins act as 'self' identification tags.

scenarios.explanation: Peripheral proteins are attached to the surface, not embedded.

scenarios.explanation: O₂ is small and nonpolar, so it diffuses straight through the bilayer.

questions.text: Which model describes the membrane as a fluid structure with embedded proteins?
questions.explanation: The fluid mosaic model describes moving proteins in a fluid bilayer.

questions.text: What is the role of cholesterol in the membrane?
questions.explanation: Cholesterol regulates fluidity; proteins do transport and recognition.

questions.text: Which part of the phospholipid is hydrophobic?
questions.explanation: The fatty-acid tails are nonpolar and hydrophobic; the phosphate head is hydrophilic.

takeaways: The plasma membrane follows the fluid mosaic model.
Phospholipids form the bilayer; proteins perform transport and signaling.
Selective permeability is the key feature of the membrane.

days.title: Passive Transport & Osmosis
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate diffusion, osmosis, and facilitated diffusion.
  • Explain how concentration gradients drive passive transport.
  • Predict the effect of tonicity on cells.
  • Relate passive transport to real-life examples.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Diffusion — movement of molecules from high to low concentration.
  • Osmosis — diffusion of water across a semipermeable membrane.
  • Facilitated diffusion — passive transport using a protein channel.
  • Tonicity — relative solute concentration of a solution.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Passive Transport Types

TypeDescriptionEnergy?
Simple diffusionSmall nonpolar molecules pass directlyNo
Facilitated diffusionUses a channel/carrier proteinNo
OsmosisWater moves through a semipermeable membraneNo

B. Tonicity

  • Isotonic — equal solute; cell stays the same.
  • Hypertonic — higher solute outside; cell shrinks (crenation).
  • Hypotonic — lower solute outside; cell swells (may lyse).

C. Real-Life Examples

  • Water absorbed by plant roots (osmosis)
  • Oxygen entering red blood cells (diffusion)
  • Glucose entering cells via GLUT transporters (facilitated diffusion)

💬 Let's Discuss

Spray perfume in one corner of a room and soon people across the room can smell it. Molecules are always moving, and they spread from where they are crowded to where they are less crowded. This is diffusion, and it is passive — no ATP is needed because the molecules move down their concentration gradient.

There are three kinds of passive transport. In simple diffusion, small nonpolar molecules (O₂, CO₂) pass directly through the lipid bilayer. In facilitated diffusion, molecules that cannot cross the bilayer — ions, glucose — still move down their gradient, but through a channel or carrier protein, such as the GLUT glucose carrier. Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane, often through water channels called aquaporins. Water moves toward the side with more solute (less free water).

To predict osmosis, compare the solution outside the cell with the inside. In a hypotonic solution (fewer solutes outside), water rushes in: animal cells swell and may burst (lyse), while plant cells become firm or turgid — which is the healthy state for plants. In a hypertonic solution (more solutes outside), water leaves: animal cells shrivel (crenate) and plant cells undergo plasmolysis, where the membrane pulls away from the wall. In an isotonic solution, there is no net movement. That is why IV fluids in hospitals are isotonic (0.9% saline), and why salting fish or making tuyo preserves it — bacteria lose water and die.

Common mistake: saying "salt moves into the cell." In osmosis, it is the water that moves, not the solute.

pairs.why: Small nonpolar molecules pass directly through the bilayer.
Osmosis is the passive movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane.

pairs.right: Uses a protein channel, no ATP
pairs.why: A protein channel or carrier helps, but no ATP is used.
Isotonic means equal solute concentration, so there is no net water movement.
Fewer solutes outside: water enters and the cell swells.
More solutes outside: water leaves and the cell shrinks.

scenarios.text: A red blood cell in pure water swells and bursts.
scenarios.explanation: Pure water is hypotonic to the cell, so water enters until it bursts.

scenarios.text: A plant wilts in saltwater.
scenarios.explanation: Saltwater is hypertonic, so water leaves the plant cells and it wilts.

scenarios.text: A cell stays the same size in a solution.
scenarios.explanation: No change in size means the solution is isotonic.

scenarios.text: Water moves into a plant root hair.
scenarios.explanation: Water moving into the root hair is osmosis.

scenarios.text: Oxygen enters a cell without a protein.
scenarios.explanation: O₂ crosses the bilayer by simple diffusion.

scenarios.text: Glucose enters via GLUT protein.
scenarios.explanation: GLUT is a carrier protein, so glucose enters by facilitated diffusion.

questions.text: Which of the following does NOT require ATP?
questions.explanation: Osmosis is passive; pumps and endocytosis need ATP.

questions.text: A cell in a hypertonic solution will:
questions.explanation: In a hypertonic solution water leaves the cell, so it shrinks.

questions.text: Facilitated diffusion differs from simple diffusion because it:
questions.explanation: Facilitated diffusion uses a protein but still moves down the gradient without ATP.

takeaways: Passive transport moves substances down a concentration gradient without ATP.
Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a semipermeable membrane.
Tonicity determines whether a cell swells, shrinks, or stays the same.
Facilitated diffusion uses proteins but no energy.

days.title: Active Transport
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Explain what active transport is.
  • Describe the sodium-potassium pump.
  • Differentiate primary from secondary active transport.
  • Relate active transport to real-life applications.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Active transport — movement against the concentration gradient using ATP.
  • Sodium-potassium pump — 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in per ATP.
  • Primary active transport — directly uses ATP.
  • Secondary active transport — uses the gradient created by primary transport.

📚 Lesson Content

A. What Is Active Transport?

Moves molecules against their concentration gradient — from low to high concentration. Requires energy (ATP).

B. The Sodium-Potassium Pump

  • Pumps 3 Na⁺ OUT of the cell
  • Pumps 2 K⁺ INTO the cell
  • Uses 1 ATP per cycle
  • Maintains resting membrane potential in nerve cells

C. Why It Matters

  • Nerve impulse transmission
  • Muscle contraction
  • Nutrient uptake in the intestine
  • Kidney function (reabsorbing nutrients)

💬 Let's Discuss

Sometimes a cell must move substances uphill — from low concentration to high concentration. That is like pushing a cart up a slope: it needs energy. Active transport uses carrier proteins called pumps and energy, usually from ATP, to move substances against their gradient.

The most famous example is the sodium–potassium pump. For each ATP used, it pushes 3 Na⁺ out and brings 2 K⁺ in. As a result, the inside of the cell stays rich in K⁺ and poor in Na⁺, and slightly negative compared with the outside. This difference, the resting membrane potential, is the stored energy that lets nerve cells fire impulses and muscle cells contract. The pump is so important that it uses about a quarter of your body's ATP — and up to two-thirds in nerve cells.

Because this pump uses ATP directly, it is primary active transport. The Na⁺ gradient it builds can then be used like water behind a dam. In secondary active transport (cotransport), Na⁺ flowing back into the cell through a carrier drags another molecule, such as glucose, in with it — even against glucose's own gradient. This is how cells lining your small intestine absorb glucose completely from digested food. Oral rehydration solution for diarrhea contains both salt and sugar for exactly this reason: the sodium–glucose cotransporter pulls water in along with them.

Compare: passive = down the gradient, no ATP; active = against the gradient, energy required. Common mistake: thinking every protein carrier means active transport. Facilitated diffusion also uses carriers but no ATP.

pairs.why: Active transport moves substances against their gradient using energy.
The pump exchanges 3 Na⁺ out for 2 K⁺ in per ATP.
Primary active transport uses ATP directly.
Secondary active transport uses an ion gradient made by a primary pump.
Nerve impulses depend on the Na⁺/K⁺ gradient the pump maintains.

scenarios.text: A molecule moves from low to high concentration.
scenarios.explanation: Moving from low to high concentration requires active transport.

scenarios.text: 3 Na⁺ exit the cell while 2 K⁺ enter.
scenarios.explanation: 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in is the Na⁺/K⁺ pump.

scenarios.text: Cell uses ATP directly for transport.
scenarios.explanation: Using ATP directly is primary active transport.

scenarios.text: A nerve cell maintains its resting potential.
scenarios.explanation: The resting potential is maintained by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump.

scenarios.text: Glucose is absorbed in the intestine against its gradient.
scenarios.explanation: Absorbing glucose against its gradient requires active transport.

scenarios.text: A cell uses a Na⁺ gradient to move another molecule.
scenarios.explanation: Using a Na⁺ gradient to move another molecule is secondary active transport.

questions.text: What does active transport require that passive transport does not?
questions.explanation: Active transport requires energy (ATP); passive transport does not.

questions.text: How many Na⁺ ions does the Na⁺/K⁺ pump move per ATP?
questions.explanation: The pump moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in for each ATP.

questions.text: Which process relies on the Na⁺/K⁺ pump?
questions.explanation: Nerve impulses depend on the ion gradients kept by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump.

takeaways: Active transport moves substances against their gradient using ATP.
The Na⁺/K⁺ pump is essential for nerve function.
Primary active transport uses ATP directly; secondary uses a gradient.
Active transport is critical for nutrient uptake and cell signaling.

days.title: Endocytosis & Exocytosis
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate endocytosis from exocytosis.
  • Distinguish phagocytosis from pinocytosis.
  • Describe receptor-mediated endocytosis.
  • Give real-life examples of bulk transport.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Endocytosis — cell takes in material via vesicles.
  • Exocytosis — cell releases material via vesicles.
  • Phagocytosis — cell engulfs large particles (cell eating).
  • Pinocytosis — cell takes in fluids (cell drinking).

📚 Lesson Content

A. Endocytosis — Three Types

TypeWhat It Takes InExample
PhagocytosisLarge particles/cellsWBC engulfing bacteria
PinocytosisFluids & small solutesIntestinal cells
Receptor-mediatedSpecific moleculesCholesterol uptake via LDL receptors

B. Exocytosis

Vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane and release contents outside.

  • Neurotransmitter release
  • Hormone secretion (insulin)
  • Mucus release
  • Waste removal

💬 Let's Discuss

Pumps and channels work for ions and small molecules, but what about a whole bacterium, a droplet of fluid, or a large protein like insulin? These are moved in bulk by wrapping them in pieces of membrane called vesicles. Bulk transport requires energy.

Endocytosis brings material into the cell. The membrane folds inward around the material and pinches off as a vesicle. There are three types. In phagocytosis ("cell eating"), the cell extends arm-like pseudopodia around a large particle. White blood cells such as macrophages and neutrophils destroy bacteria this way; the vesicle then fuses with a lysosome that digests its contents. In pinocytosis ("cell drinking"), the cell takes in small droplets of extracellular fluid with whatever is dissolved in it — not selective. In receptor-mediated endocytosis, only molecules that bind specific receptors are taken in. Cells absorb cholesterol from blood this way by grabbing LDL particles. People with faulty LDL receptors cannot remove cholesterol from their blood and develop heart disease early (familial hypercholesterolemia).

Exocytosis is the reverse: vesicles from the Golgi move to the membrane, fuse with it, and release their contents outside. Pancreatic cells secrete insulin and digestive enzymes, and neurons release neurotransmitters at synapses, by exocytosis. Each time, the vesicle's membrane becomes part of the plasma membrane, which is also how the cell adds new membrane.

Memory aid: endo = enter, exo = exit. Common mistake: thinking endocytosis uses channel proteins. It uses vesicles.

pairs.why: Endocytosis brings material into the cell inside vesicles.
Exocytosis releases material when vesicles fuse with the membrane.
Phagocytosis engulfs large particles such as bacteria.
Pinocytosis takes in small droplets of fluid.
Receptor-mediated endocytosis takes in only molecules that bind specific receptors.

scenarios.text: A white blood cell engulfs a bacterium.
scenarios.explanation: Engulfing a whole bacterium is phagocytosis.

scenarios.text: A cell takes in extracellular fluid.
scenarios.explanation: Taking in fluid droplets is pinocytosis.

scenarios.text: Insulin is released from a pancreatic cell.
scenarios.explanation: Releasing insulin to the outside is exocytosis.

scenarios.text: Cholesterol is taken in via LDL receptors.
scenarios.explanation: LDL binds specific receptors — receptor-mediated endocytosis.

scenarios.text: A neuron releases neurotransmitters.
scenarios.explanation: Neurotransmitters leave in vesicles by exocytosis.

scenarios.text: A cell expels waste through vesicles.
scenarios.explanation: Expelling wastes in vesicles is exocytosis.

questions.text: What is the difference between endocytosis and exocytosis?
questions.explanation: Endocytosis brings material in; exocytosis sends it out — they differ in direction.

questions.text: Which process involves engulfing large particles?
Which of the following is an example of exocytosis?
questions.explanation: Insulin is secreted by exocytosis; the other choices bring material into the cell.

takeaways: Endocytosis brings material IN; exocytosis releases material OUT.
Phagocytosis = cell eating; pinocytosis = cell drinking.
Exocytosis is essential for secretion and waste removal.
